title: Influence Maximization via Graph Neural Bandits

problem.claim: Influence maximization must maximize the number of distinct influenced users over multiple diffusion rounds when the diffusion network topology is only partially known.

gap.claim: The influence maximization setting lacks sufficient knowledge of the underlying diffusion network, creating a need to balance exploration and exploitation.

contributions.claim: The authors propose IM-GNB, a framework that estimates users' probabilities of being influenced by diffusion seeds.
IM-GNB constructs exploitation and exploration graphs from the initial estimates and uses GCNs to select seed nodes in real time while refining estimated rewards.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on two large real-world datasets.
The authors report that IM-GNB significantly improves diffusion-campaign spread compared with baseline methods when the underlying network is unknown.

narrative_sequence.summary: The study addresses influence maximization with limited knowledge of diffusion-network topology in a multi-round campaign.
The authors combine bandit exploration-exploitation with neural-network expressivity and propose the IM-GNB framework.
The framework builds exploitation and exploration graphs, then uses GCNs to select seeds in real time and refine rewards.
Experiments on two large real-world datasets are reported to show improved spread over baseline methods.

source_observation.claim: The framework separates estimated influence information into exploitation and exploration graphs before real-time seed selection.

interpretation.claim: Separating exploitation and exploration representations may help organize decision-making when network structure is uncertain.

application.claim: Use separate representations for exploiting current estimates and exploring uncertain network structure in adaptive diffusion campaigns.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this separation is beneficial outside the reported influence-maximization setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or quantitative improvements.
The abstract does not describe the bandit objective, training procedure, or theoretical guarantees.
The abstract does not establish independent verification or reproducibility.
